draft.title: River health in the basin
card: River health describes how well a river and its wetlands support plants, animals and people. In the Murray-Darling Basin, several human actions have lowered it.
Taking large amounts of water for use on farms and in towns leaves less water in the rivers. Wetlands can dry out, and low flows can leave fish and other water life short of habitat.
Dams and weirs change when and how much water flows downstream. Clearing land can raise salt levels, because removing deep-rooted plants lets more water seep underground and bring salt up.
Warm, slow, low water with extra nutrients can cause algal blooms. Blooms can use up oxygen in the water, which can lead to fish kills.
draft.remember: Less water, changed flows and cleared land can harm rivers, causing salinity, blooms, fish kills and drying wetlands.

a.q: Which change is most likely to lead to an algal bloom in a river of the basin?
opts: Warm, slow, low water with extra nutrients
Fast, cold water flowing from a dam release
A wetland filling with water after rain
Deep-rooted trees planted along the bank
a.why: Algal blooms are more likely when water is warm, slow and low and has extra nutrients. Fast, cold flow is the tempting wrong choice because it mixes and moves the water, so it does not give blooms the same conditions.
a.clue: Think about water that is warm and barely moving.

b.q: Farmers near a river in the basin clear all the deep-rooted trees from their paddocks. Over time, which effect is most likely?
opts: More salt rising in the soil and reaching the river
More water being taken straight from the river
Fewer dams changing the timing of river flows
Wetlands staying full because less water seeps down
b.why: Without deep-rooted plants, more water seeps underground and can bring salt up, so salinity can rise. Taking water from the river is a different cause of poor river health, and clearing land does not make it happen.
b.clue: Ask what deep roots do to the water underground.

a.best: Warm, slow, low water with extra nutrients

b.best: More salt rising in the soil and reaching the river

problems.detail: The right option stands out. It is the longest and the only one with several precise conditions, and it copies the card's wording word for word. A student could pick it without understanding why blooms form.
The clue ('water that is warm and barely moving') points straight at the only option describing warm, slow water, which gives the answer away.
